Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): I am speaking to the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) at the conclusion of his speech this afternoon. In doing so I propose to speak in more temperate language than was used by him, with a greater sense of responsibility than was evident in his concluding remarks, and with a more scrupulous regard for the realities of the situation which confronts our country.
Why was this amendment introduced in the form in which it has been presented to this house? Was it because the leader of the opposition was convinced in his own heart and mind that there has not been a marked improvement in the employment situation in this country during the past year? To that question me only answer can be an emphatic negative. The evidence of economic improvement in Canada does not need to be adduced in the form of elaborate statistics. That improvement is evidenced in practically every statement issued by the bureau of statistics within the past year, by the statements which have been issued and circulated throughout this country by bank presidents, by heads of mortgage corporations, and by those who by reason of their

The Budget-Mr. Rogers

interests and their particular knowledge of different phases of industrial life in this country are competent to speak with authority. There can be no question whatsoever that the employment situation in Canada at this time is substantially better than it was a year ago, and very much better indeed than it was at any time during the period when hon. gentlemen opposite were charged with the administration of this country.
Was this amendment introduced, sir, because the leader of the opposition had some constructive suggestion to offer after five years of extravagant futility, in attempting to deal with a problem which he said he would solve or perish in the attempt? I leave it to the judgment of the house whether in anything that was said by the right hon. gentleman this afternoon there was the slightest suggestion of any constructive effort which might assist in dealing with this grave national problem. The one compelling reason for the amendment, as given to this house in the concluding remarks of the leader of the opposition, was briefly this, that he had proposed this amendment because it was the same sort of amendment the Liberal opposition had proposed when his own administration was in power. In other words the leader of the opposition has decided first to misrepresent the unemployment situation in this country and then, to use it for the purpose of political reprisal.
I doubt if the records of this house will disclose a more inappropriate amendment to a budget speech or one based upon a more flagrant distortion or misunderstanding of the facts. The leader of the opposition based his amendment chiefly upon a recital of the appointments made to the staff of the National Employment Commission. I shall deal with that aspect of the matter in a few moments, but I have too keen an interest in the problem of unemployment and too high a regard for the appreciation of that problem by the members of this house to subordinate the larger considerations of unemployment policy to a discussion of an aspect of the matter which after all does not go to the root of the question. This administration has been in office since October, 1935. When the late administration came into office it did so on the basis of the most emphatic pledges given by the leader of the Conservative party that he would end unemployment; that he would provide work and not doles; that he would blast his way into the markets of the world. When he came into power on his own statement the number of unemployed in this country was
117.000.	When the present administration

assumed office and the right hon. gentleman left it, in October of 1935, according to the bureau of statistics the number of unemployed had risen to 435,000. In case there should be any misapprehension as to the improvement that has taken place during the past year at this point I should like to say-and I propose to deal with it more fully later-that the figures of the bureau of statistics for October, 1936, are not 435,000 but 393,000, which I submit is a very substantial reduction in that period of time.
What was the situation when this government came into power? What was the situation as between the dominion government and the provincial governments? Were those relations based upon harmony or were they not shot through with friction from one end of this dominion to the other? What was the attitude of the younger people? What was the attitude that was engendered in the relief camps which were established by the late administration, more or less, I suggest, as a counsel of despair, and which provided as it were a chain of hostels for the unemployed from Nova Scotia to British Columbia? I do not think I need remind hon. members that those relief camps, which at that time had been in existence for a number of years, harboured men of ages varying from eighteen to sixty; men who had not found the work that had been promised them by the leader of the opposition in 1930; men who found in ' those camps nothing more than a shelter against the storm. Those who entered the relief camps at that time assuredly carried nothing in with them, and with equal assurance it can be said that those who left the relief camps carried nothing out. The camps were organized on the basis of a payment of twenty cents a day to those in them. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the relief camps we found when we came into office were nothing more or less than a blind alley for the unemployed. For the government they were an extravagant luxury. In the final year of their operation the total cost was over $9,000,000. If in the succeeding year they had been continued on the existing basis the cost would have risen to $12,000,000; that is, on the basis of the increased wage allowance which was put into effect by this administration.
First of all I want to say, to make it clear beyond peradventure, that when this government came into office and I first went to the Department of Labour there was no problem that gave me keener concern than the plight of those single unemployed men in the relief camps of this country. I had a strong feeling.

The Budget-Mr. Rogers
based upon my knowledge of conditions in those relief camps and my knowledge of the sense of frustration and despair which was developed by them, that the best way to deal with the relief camps was to close them as quickly as possible. On the other hand, in this case not following the policy which on occasion, I suggest, was followed by the leader of the opposition, it seemed to me that we should not make our judgment blindly; that we should get some collective thought upon this problem and, through collective thought, find some definite objective, some determined road. So we appointed a committee to investigate relief camps in Canada, and that committee, I suggest, was composed of men who had not only a keen appreciation of all the problems involved in the administration of relief camps but who also had an equally keen appreciation of the human elements involved. On that commission we had the head of the employment service of Canada; we had Mr. Humphrey Mitchell, a former member of this house, and we had a man who had not been closely connected with government in other years but for whom I have a very high regard, Doctor Bradwin, president of the Frontier college. These men made their investigation and in due course presented their report. The report confirmed the view which I suggested a moment ago I had formed in my own mind as to the disposition that should be made of the camps. They proposed that these camps should be closed as soon as possible. They stated in the most emphatic terms that unless they were closed they would tend to become institutionalized, and that in their opinion the relief camps in their structure, and particularly in the attitude of mind which they developed in the youth of this country, were alien to the spirit of this young dominion.
So, upon the basis of that report, we determined to close the relief camps, and we set a date as an objective. Almost a year ago we declared that we believed it would be possible to close the relief camps by July 1 of last year. I do not hesitate to tell the house that there were those who said it could not be done, that it would lead to riots, to disturbances and to a serious dislocation of business. Despite those forebodings we felt that our objective was correct, and because we believed that we believed also that the way would be found to realize it. It was so arranged that through the provision of employment upon special maintenance work on the railways, about 10,000 of the men in the relief camps were given an opportunity for employment in the summer months at the prevailing rates of wages for the type of work it 31111-90i
was proposed they should do. Almost 1,000 others were absorbed into farm employment. Many others, through the assistance of the employment service, found employment in other directions. As I have said, the camps were closed, and about 10,000 of the men in them were transferred to remunerative employment. To this time the camps have not been reopened.
Naturally at t'he conclusion of the work upon the railways during the past summer the government was confronted with the issue of what next should be done to deal with the single unemployed. In our decision as to what should be done I should like to make it clear that the government had the advice and the very useful assistance of the National Employment Commission, which this afternoon was condemned by the leader of the opposition. We believed it would create a much more wholesome atmosphere for the single unemployed and transients in various parts of the country if we could direct them into employment connected with the great primary industries of the dominion. In conjunction with the provinces we worked out the details of the farm employment scheme. I should like to make it very clear that in the conception and execution of the farm employment plan the National Employment Commission was of the utmost assistance to the government.
I have before me figures covering farm placements in the last few months. Some 46.000 placements have been made under the farm employment plan in the various provinces where it is in use. I have it on good authority that in Saskatchewan there is not a single unemployed man now available for farm employment service. I also have-

If I had it now, I would give it with equal readiness. I should say however that the present scheme is a development of a previous scheme, and in my own mind that is one of the merits of it. After all, we have sought to learn by experience in dealing with unemployment. Unfortunately there was not as much record of the experience of hon. members opposite as one could have wished, but so far as the
The Budget-Mr. Rogers

scheme was in operation and had proved to have merit, we built upon it. I think we can say we have improved upon some features of it.

As I have said, under the farm employment plan,-and the supplementary plans, under which some 5.000 additional men were employed, particularly in forestry work in British Columbia and Manitoba-during the last few months there have been placements of some 50,000 men. Previously there was an aimless, drifting group of single unemployed men in various parts of the country, and more particularly in the western provinces.
I am not speaking about something of which I am ignorant. Fortunately some months ago I had the opportunity of travelling through western Canada. I have seen the single unemployed at their work on the railways. I have talked with them; I have seen them gathered in queues at soup kitchens in Winnipeg and Edmonton. I know something of what years of insecurity and idleness have done to their morale, and I suggest the leader of the opposition would have been far more sensible of his responsibility at this time if, instead of holding up to this house the record of staff appointments to the National Employment Commission, thereby suggesting that the government had not dealt with the great national problem, he had at least touched upon some of the details, some of the broad principles lying at the base of the policies we have put into effect.
Another problem which confronted the government when it came into office was the relationship between the dominion and the provinces and municipalities, particularly with respect to the exact apportionment of costs of unemployment relief. I shall not go into the historical background of that aspect of the unemployment problem. However I do want to make it as clear as possible to the house that, by reason of the very structure of our government under the federal constitution, there is, as it were, inherent antagonism always capable of being brought to a head, oecause of the apportionment of financial responsibilities in relation not only to unemployment relief but to social services generally.
When we took office we found the provinces and municipalities believed they were facing a very serious crisis if the dominion

government at that time did not give them further assistance-and remember that at that time sentiment and economic conditions in Canada were quite different from what they are to-day-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And only sixteen months ago.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Sometimes I wonder if we realize the extraordinary change that has taken place within the last few months, particularly in respect to the sentiment of the people. At that time many provinces and municipalities harboured the well-grounded fear that if they did not receive a greater degree of assistance from the dominion government in connection with unemployment relief they would be forced into bankruptcy. Again we did not make our judgment blindly; rather we called the provinces into conference and discussed the matter with them. Upon the basis of what they told us, and of what came to us from the mayors' conference which met in Montreal at about the same time, we decided it was in the interests of a proper administration of unemployment relief, and in the interests of maintaining a proper relationship between the dominion and the provinces, that at least during the critical period the dominion should assume a larger proportion of the costs for unemployment relief. We acted accordingly.
As a result of that action I believe pressure upon many municipalities was lifted. As a result of it the serious pressure on some of the western provinces, which had been felt through years of drought, was relieved. Through that action we established a basis for a much more satisfactory handling of some of the broader aspects of unemployment and relief. Subsequently when we believed the greatest pressure had been relieved we determined that there should be a downward adjustment of relief grants from the dominion to the provinces, and we have followed that policy carefully. In getting the problem into a clearer perspective we are at this time receiving the assistance of the National Employment Commission. It has been announced that by reason of the marked economic recovery in the past year the dominion government is now entitled to accept a lesser degree of financial responsibility for unemployment relief. Here again I would emphasize that we are proceeding along the lines of making these readjustments upon some rational basis and in such a way as to ensure for us the continued cooperation of the provinces and the municipalities.

The Budget-Mr. Rogers
I would not suggest for one moment to this house that the problem of unemployment and relief, either in its human or its financial aspect, can be liquidated1 within a few months. I know something, as I think all members of this house do, of what might be termed the residual problems of the economic shock through which this country has been passing since 1930. There are great and grave problems of readjustment. There is not merely the restoration of morale among the single unemployed-that in itself is a most serious and important matter-but there is also the providing of the means by which these young men who have perforce lived a life of idleness in recent years can gradually be brought back into the economic life of this country in a manner to enable them to recover their independence and their self-respect. That is our objective; that is our determined road.
When we came into office we found that the government of the day had made a practice of cooperating with the provinces in works programs designed as a measure of relief for unemployment. In making our arrangements with the provinces during the past year we inserted in the agreements for the first time a clause requiring that a specific proportion of the number employed upon these works should be taken from the relief rolls. We worked on the principle, which I believe is a sound one, that relief works should reduce relief rolls. If relief works do not reduce relief rolls, they are misnamed and I doubt the wisdom of continuing them.
I do not suggest that hon. gentlemen opposite were oblivious to this aspect of the question. I would not suggest for one moment that they were not equally anxious to deal with it. There is no such thing as a monopoly of human sympathy and compassion. We may differ in our policies, but I doubt whether any of us in this house differ greatly in our desire to deal in the most satisfactory way with this matter of unemployment and relief. At the same time, the previous agreements with the provinces did not stipulate that a fixed percentage of those employed on these works should be taken from relief rolls. We made that stipulation. Forty thousand men were employed upon these works during the past year and at least 20.000 were taken from the relief rolls, thus reducing the burden on municipalities from one end of the dominion to the other.
I come now to the issue, if we can call it such, raised by the leader of the opposition this afternoon. I wonder if the right hon. gentleman appreciated fully the example in dialectic he gave the younger members of this
house, myself included. The right hon. gentleman was introducing an amendment regretting that this government had failed to deal adequately with the unemployment problem, and three-quarters of his discussion of the unemployment problem was a recital of staff appointments to the National Employment Commission. I am going to deal with that question here and now, having first discussed the broad considerations of policy which to my mind should have been dealt with by the leader of the opposition.
The National Employment Commission was set up last year under legislation passed by this parliament. That legislation provided for a commission of seven members and for two advisory committees, one known as the youth employment committee and the other as the women's employment committee. I do not think anyone who has given any study to the problem of unemployment relief can fail to realize that these two committees were called upon to deal with what might very properly be termed special and all-important aspects of the question. Provision was made in the act for the payment of such fees and travelling expenses as might be decided upon by the governor in council. Two members of the employment commission have served without remuneration, and one of these was only reimbursed for his travelling expenses. Only three members of the commission may be said to have given nearly all of their time to the work of the commission in recent months. The youth employment committee has been making a study of its particular problem only in quite recent months, and the same may be said of the women's employment committee. This commission did not differ actually in structure from other commissions which frequently have been appointed in this country to deal with problems less grave.
I have here a complete statement of the total expenses of the National Employment Commission to date. I propose to place these before the house in order that there may be no misunderstanding as to what this commission has cost this country up to the present time. In doing this I should like again to object to the method employed by the leader of the opposition to create an impression contrary to the facts. I am not suggesting that he knew the information he gave was contrary to the facts, but there was no doubt as to the impression he sought to convey. He read lists of names which were repeated time and again.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am ill prepared at the moment to deal effectively with the important issue brought to the fore in this debate by the amendment and by the remarks of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). Nevertheless as I listened to the minister's remarks I felt that certain claims advanced by him should not pass unchallenged. I consider it my duty on this occasion at least to give the evidence that has come into my possession with regard to the circumstances of single unemployed men in this country, and particularly in British Columbia-evidence which has been gained through close and intimate
The Budget-Mr. MacNeil

contact with these men during the latter part of last summer and during the autumn of 1936. I consider it not only a privilege but a duty to advance a plea on behalf of these single homeless young men and women, and to direct the attention of the house to the fact that the statistics do not tell the whole story. It is most unfortunate that on this occasion the minister should have been compelled merely to defend the work of the employment commission on the basis of the statistics which have been secured. I propose to deal with this matter from the standpoint of human values rather than that of statistics.
I was present in the house when, last session, the minister dealt with the problem of the young men then in relief camps across the dominion. He announced that on July 1, 1936; it would be possible to close the relief camps, and that he had a solution in view. He proposed to solve the unemployment problem of . these young men with the plans he was then about to table; he said they were on the road to success, that he was going to place them on a work and wages basis during the summer months, and he tabled the agreements entered into with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian National Railway Company. I regard it as most unfortunate that during last session we had not sufficient time properly to analyze the terms of these agreements. Even the terminology employed was most unfortunate. It recites that His Majesty's government proposed then to "deliver" approximately ten thousand young men, able and willing to work, to the railway companies, these young men to be subject to dismissal for cause and required to accept the discipline imposed upon all the other extra gang labourers. The phrasing was most unfortunate, reminding one of the old indentures of bondage; and a form of bondage it proved to be, for these men were actually "delivered," ushered out of the relief camps and delivered to the railway companies, and when any of them attempted to escape the servitude imposed upon them by the terms of these agreements they were almost branded as criminals.
At the same time the minister gave solemn assurance that the railway companies would undertake extra maintenance of way and betterment work; that they would not attempt to replace the regular maintenance crews with the men from the relief camps. From personal observation I must say that this assurance was violated at many points by the railway companies. Men taken from the relief camps were placed on regular maintenance

work; they displaced the regular maintenance crews in many districts across this country, and were required to do heavy maintenance work for which they were poorly prepared.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. member will permit me, I do not feel that I should allow that statement to pass without some correction. We obtained definite assurances that the work done by the men who came from the relief camps was in excess of the normal maintenance work being undertaken by the railways during the past summer. Subsequently we received assurance that not only was that true, but that the additional maintenance program which was inaugurated with these men from the relief camps made possible the employment of about two thousand railway men who theretofore had been unemployed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am well aware that the minister received that assurance from the railway companies. I am also aware that at the time those agreements were to be carried out, the minister, in the performance of his duties, was absent from the country. But I may tell hon. members that in visiting the small towns in the interior of British Columbia, and even on the prairies, many men told me that for the first time they were compelled to go on relief because they had been released from the regular maintenance work on the railways, work upon which they had depended season after season for their livelihood, to make way for the men from the relief camps. I submit that the evidence is that only too many men on regular maintenance crews were displaced by men from the relief camps. May I also point out that many of these men, when I questioned them, swore that they left the relief camps prior to the date of these agreements to which I have referred, hoping to secure employment on the regular maintenance crews; that they did secure such employment and while engaged in that work were discharged when the men from the relief camps appeared on the scene. They were unable subsequently to get employment with the extra gangs. The evidence through the prairie towns and the towns in the interior of British Columbia pointed conclusive]}' to the fact that the railway companies violated the terms of the agreement in that respect.
The minister stated at the time that the men would be placed upon a work and wages basis. Upon investigation it was found that work and wages meant working ten hours a day for twenty-five cents an hour, in spite of the terms of the agreement.

The Budget-Mr. MocNeil

speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt, but if my hon. friend will permit me, I have here a report of the work, and I think this ought to be corrected, for it is important. Our information is that in addition to those actually employed on the maintenance of way work the total number of those employed under the terms of the agreement in supervision, operating steam shovels and work trains, and paid directly by the railways was, for the Canadian Pacific Railway, 1,132, and for the Canadian National Railways, 1,000, a total of 2.132.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I cannot see that those figures upset the argument I am advancing. I repeat that my information was gleaned from the men themselves who testified that they were actually doing regular maintenance work, from men who were actually released from employment on regular maintenance crews, and those who were in charge of relief and welfare activities in the various towns to which I have referred.
I stress the point of work and wages. The agreements were worded in such a way as to offer loopholes which under the conditions which prevailed were taken full advantage of by the railway companies. In only too many instances the men worked day after day for ten hours a day at the rate of twenty-five cents an hour, doing heavy arduous work for which they were poorly prepared, and in many gangs men were dropping right and left through exhaustion. Only too many men who were casualties were compelled to leave the gangs before the termination of the period of employment, and subsequently were discriminated against in the provinces in which they applied for relief. This work and wages basis of twenty-five cents an hour was in direct violation of the laws regulating working conditions and wages in some provinces.
Under the terms of the agreement the railway companies were to receive reimbursement for wages so paid up to a sum not exceeding $3,000,000. According to the statistics tabled by the minister this session, approximately $2,600,000 was paid under these conditions. In addition the railway companies were to receive a loan of approximately a million dollars to sweeten the bargain. I cannot refrain from bringing to the attention of the government and hon. members the effects of this agreement, chiefly because the minister at that time emphasized the importance of relying upon private enterprise for a solution of this problem. What happened as a result of this reliance on private enterprise? It certainly was a grand deal for someone, but not for the men. The railways got a straight gift of approximately $3,000,000 worth of
work performed; the men got increased hardships and faced destitution at the opening of last winter. In addition the railways received reimbursement for transportation in moving gangs back and forth. It was arranged that they should receive reimbursement for medical aid, and deductions were made from that pitiful pay of twenty-five cents an hour for board, lodging, blankets, and medical aid. The maximum term of employment was something like 1,248 hours, and I defy any hon. member, taking the maximum wages that might be received by any individual and deducting therefrom the amounts charged by the railways for board and lodging, blankets, medical aid, et cetera, to arrive at a sum that would keep body and soul together for the succeeding winter. In fact I found on personal investigation that many men left the gangs with sums not in excess of $30 or $40, and those who were able to work the full time left with very little in excess of $100. Out of this they were required to pay their own transportation back to the points from which they came. So that it was not in any sense a solution of the unemployment problem as affecting these young men.
Towards the end of the summer I happened to be in the interior of British Columbia, and everywhere I saw these young men on the freight trains passing through the divisional points with their meagre belongings in small packs on their backs, working their way along, endeavouring to secure employment in the harvest fields, or a little later in the apple orchards of the Okanagan, or the tomato fields, and then moving on towards the coast in the hope of securing employment in the woods of British Columbia. They were making an earnest endeavour to gain whatever benefits were possible from casual employment on the prairies and in the interior of British Columbia as opportunities arose, following this casual employment from district to district. Everywhere they were establishing little jungle camps as bases of operations, following, shall I say, the lure of propaganda appearing in the newspapers at that time to the effect that at many points in British Columbia unemployment no longer existed. They had every inducement to move in that direction because of the advertising carried in the daily press with regard to the prosperity of various sections of British Columbia.
Subsequently a large number of these young men gathered in Vancouver. They were unable to secure employment, unable to get relief, because in moving from relief camps to the work on extra gangs, and subsequently in search of casual employment, under the regulations they were deprived of all rights
The Budget-Mr. MacNeil

of domicile. It was estimated at one time that something like 3,000 young men were footloose in Vancouver. In an effort to present their claims to the authorities they organized. Being without work and unable to obtain relief they were facing destitution. It has been alleged that these activities were fostered by subversive organizations. My investigation of the matter led me to a different conclusion. I found these young men organizing in a very efficient and democratic way, meeting almost daily, electing their own leaders by the usual democratic procedure, and determining their own policy. From my knowledge of the calibre of these young men I say that they were not of the type that might easily be led by persons actuated by ulterior motives. Mainly they were recruited from the cities of eastern Canada, boys from seventeen to twenty-five years of age, who had not formed any very definite opinions with regard to political policies and were simply seeking some opportunity of solving their own acute problem. They organized and attempted to make representations to the authorities. The civic authorities were unable to accept any responsibility. For that I cannot blame them, because they were faced with a large number of men for whom they could not provide. The provincial government likewise denied any responsibility, and representations were made day after day to the federal government asking that some action be taken to deal effectively with this problem. No effective answer could be secured. The men were desperate. They attempted to organize an appeal to the public of Vancouver, and on one occasion they marched to Hamilton hall, where single men received their relief. There an unfortunate riot occurred. I cannot with propriety comment on the circumstances of that riot, which have been dealt with by the courts of the land, but of this I am convinced: in planning to present their claims in Hamilton hall the men originally did not intend to engage in or incite a riot. Unfortunately two young men were sentenced to spend two years in the penitentiary as a result of that disturbance.
The organized group proceeded to place their case before the public in Vancouver. They appeared on street corners soliciting alms, holding out tin cans with signs stating that they were homeless, without work and without relief. The public of Vancouver responded very generously, but for reasons best known to themselves the civic authorities decided that this was a breach of the law. and the men were arrested in large groups.

Day after day, thirty, forty or fifty men would be picked up, taken to the police station and charged in the Vancouver police court. They may have been guilty of a technical breach of the law; usually they were charged with vagrancy under section (d) of the vagrancy section of the criminal code, but actually their only crime was that they were without food and shelter and without opportunity for employment, and that they had the courage to state their needs in a public place. Up to that time no response had been received from the federal government; no escape from their predicament had been offered. They had no recourse, actually, but to take the course that was taken, to appeal publicly and in an organized way for funds. The funds so secured were handled in a businesslike and efficient way; they were distributed among the men in such a manner as to provide each man with two meals a day and a bed.
Subsequently I was invited by the men themselves to appear on their behalf in the Vancouver police court. In attempting to carry on this work I interrogated the men individually and gained a close knowledge of the circumstances and life history of each man. I have these records under my hand, the lists of the Vancouver police court and my notes taken in each individual case. I mention that to show that I have definite knowledge of their circumstances. Of the large number of young men I interviewed approximately seventy per cent were Canadians, from good Canadian homes, and the majority of these were from eastern Canada. A small percentage of the men had come from the United Kingdom, encouraged to do so under various immigration schemes. They were denied the right of domicile in British Columbia. An attempt was being made to compel them to accept transportation to other points in Canada, but at that time no assurance was given to any man that if he accepted that transportation he would fare any better at his destination. For the majority of them to accept such transportation would have been suicide. They had no clothes except those in which they stood, usually consisting merely of a pair of pants, a shirt and a sweater. It would have been suicidal for them to facp the severity of winter in eastern Canada in such garb.

speechtext: No boots or socks?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Halifax inquires as to their boots and socks. Very few of these men had socks, and after they had tramped through the Okanagan in search of work the condition of their boots beggared description.

The Budget-Mr. MacNeil
Approximately 140 men were sentenced in the Vancouver police court to varying terms of imprisonment ranging from two months to six months. That was before I appeared in court on their behalf. When I interviewed the police magistrate, the chief of police and others concerned, all of whom offered me their very courteous cooperation, they stated very clearly not once but several times, publicly from the bench, that this was not a crime problem. They did not desire to deal with it as a crime problem; it was a problem of unemployment which never should have been referred to the police authorities. They were looking anxiously for some solution, and at that time they stated that they were making the most emphatic representations to the federal government asking that definite action should be taken. Day after day the men were arrested and charged in police court. Through the cooperation of the social welfare agencies temporary maintenance was secured. When I could assure the police magistrate that temporary maintenance would be provided the men were released on their own recognizance pending action by the federal government. Those who had arrived in the city of Vancouver only a few weeks previously were sentenced; an additional sixty men were sent to Oakalla prison farm.
The ironical and tragic part of it was that when these men were questioned in court it was represented that they had the opportunity of taking advantage of the farm placement scheme. The magistrate would say, "Are you willing to accept work on a farm at $5 a month and your board? If you stay long enough you will probably get $750 and your board." At that time no provision had been made in the province of British Columbia for the employment under the farm placement scheme of men whose domicile in that province had not been established under the regulations, nor was any assurance given those men that if they accepted transportation to any point elsewhere in Canada they would be given employment under that scheme elsewhere. Furthermore, as subsequently disclosed, at that time no definite agreement had been arrived at with the province of British Columbia in respect to a farm placement scheme. As a matter of fact a survey of the farmers in that province had been made, and only approximately fifty-five farmers stated that they could possibly employ men under the terms indicated in the proposed agreement.
So, through the cooperation of the social welfare agencies in the city of Vancouver, and to some extent with the provincial government, temporary maintenance was provided. Several hundred men at that time were rescued from going to gaol. Later, when the minister returned from Europe and visited the city of Vancouver, I must say as very much to his credit that he received the men with courtesy and sympathy, and within twenty-four hours announced to them that he had entered into a special agreement with the provincial government relating to forestry projects. The men accepted the agreement. They were somewhat discouraged by its terms, but nevertheless they accepted it; they immediately registered, received temporary relief and thousands were placed in employment on the forestry projects. But something like 160 young men continued to serve their terms of imprisonment in Oakalla, The delay of the federal government resulted in that tragedy. They were compelled to associate and fraternize with hardened criminals from the underworld. Not once but several times I had definite evidence that young men from good Canadian homes in the east were approached by hardened criminals and asked to engage in the easier life of crime. I consider that a great tragedy.
I mention this to-night because in a way it dramatizes that which has been happening to the young men for whom the minister claims adequate provision has been made. They are now engaged in the forestry projects of British Columbia, and are not securing the advantages of training. I think it may reasonably be suggested that men engaged in forestry work should be given the advantage of technical training in the science of forestation. Adequate facilities exist for such training. Nevertheless they are engaged under distressing conditions merely in the arduous work of clearing trails, most of which lead to valuable mining properties and various timber limits now operated by large interests in British Columbia. The men are not yet on a work and wages basis. It is true that for each day they work they receive a larger wage than they formerly did in the relief camps under the Conservative administration, but when we consider the wages paid and the period for which these wages must provide we find that they are working for a sum actually no greater than the amount they would receive if, in the province of British Columbia, they were granted the relief to which a single man is entitled.
The relief camps are not closed; many of the camps in British Columbia have been reopened. In the constituency I represent the camps which were operating prior to
The Budget-Mr. MacNeil

July 1, 1936, are again operating under practically the same conditions, and the men are engaged in exactly the same work as before. Slightly different arrangements exist as to the payment of wages, but they still work at relief rates without any hope for the future and without any solution of their problems. My information is that those who have accepted placement under the farm placement scheme are in an equally hopeless position. Even as before, they are suffering frustration and hopelessness with regard to the future.
It would be grossly unfair if I did not mention the single homeless women. It has been forcibly brought to my attention that the plight of single homeless women is even more serious. Upon investigation I have found there had been a similar migration of young women to the coast, particularly from the burnt out areas in the prairie provinces. Upon application to the various social welfare agencies some secured meals and shelter for a couple of days, but after that time they were cast out. They were denied relief by the provincial authorities. Although so far as the men were concerned the minister accepted responsibility for waiving the regulations as regards domicile in British Columbia, enabling all those in the province prior to November 15, 1936, to receive the advantages of forestry work, no equivalent provision was made for the young women who took part in the same migration. Their plight was pitiful in the extreme. Incident after incident was brought to my attention of young women from good homes and of excellent character who had to spend night after night in railway depots, who had to wander here and there begging for employment and living under most tragic circumstances. No provision could be secured for them, because they could not establish domicile in any particular province. They fell between two stools because of the dispute as to responsibility which was carried on between federal and provincial authorities. They were left as outcasts.
While I would not suggest that the character of the majority of these young women could be questioned-in fact I have reason to believe the great majority were of excellent character -it is nevertheless true that failure to deal adequately with the problem has contributed seriously to other problems. My conclusions on that score are corroborated by people holding official positions. The problem of the unmarried mothers is becoming more acute; the problem of illicit alliances is more acute, as all social welfare workers know. Young girls compelled to leave their homes in eastern Canada and in the prairie provinces are panhandling, as we say, on the

skid-road for a meal, and the price of a bed. It is a most pitiful situation. Furthermore, the problem of venereal disease is becoming more acute, as many are unable to obtain treatment. No doubt this economic situation is a contributing factor to the serious aggravation of social problems. The fact that disturbs me is that young women on every hand are being exploited in the most vicious fashion by unscrupulous employers. It is well known that there is a chain of protected bawdy houses throughout the interior of British Columbia, and that the recruiting of inmates for these houses is being conducted in certain sections of Vancouver city from among this class of women.
I should be remiss in my duty if I did not make a most earnest appeal to the federal authorities to accept responsibility for the protection of young women who find themselves in these unfortunate circumstances. I have said that the relief camps are not closed, and that the plight of the young homeless men is as serious as it was on July 1 of last year. I believe the minister was not quite fair to himself or to the work in hand when he claimed so substantial a measure of improvement. When we delve beneath the surface, when we contact human beings in circumstances with which they must contend and when we actually interrogate men and women we realize their plight is as serious as it was before, and that never was it so imperative that definite action be taken.
In many sections of British Columbia the relief camps are operating on exactly the same basis as before. Young men are without hope. The work is not even as well organized as it was before. No assurance has been given that upon the conclusion of work on these projects they will be cared for. Worst of all, the measure of recovery which is claimed by the minister has not provided any large measure of additional employment opportunities for these young men. They are without training; they are eager; they are keen, and they are of a good type, generally speaking, but they have not had the advantage of equipping themselves mentally or physically for employment opportunities, if such opportunities should be offered by employers of labour. This is particularly true of the young women. Under the minister's present policy and the plans which have been sketched for the benefit of the house they are largely the victims of unscrupulous exploitation by employers of labour. They are being used, as cheap labour, to the disadvantage of other workers and, worst of all, they are being denied the opportunities they have a right to expect from this nation.

speechtext:
pointed out a few of the danger signals which should be observed. I shall defer my remarks on this matter until the main motion is being discussed, but I should like to suggest that as these danger signals have something to do with unemployment they should receive consideration. They are all around us. They are present on the stock market. There is a fixed price for gold; the costs of production are rising day by day and there is bound to be a collapse in that direction if we are not careful. The production of armaments cannot go on indefinitely, and when it slows down, look out for trouble. Perhaps the minister was wise in reducing his works program, but he had better get ready for another works program. He had better continue the policy of taking relief workers off the relief roll. Of that I shall say something a little later.
I come now to the main subject. We were supposed to find something within the confines of this budget to help the unemployment situation. Not finding it in any degree, but rather finding something which retarded employment, we moved an amendment to the main motion. There are a number of reasons why I propose to vote for the amendment, some of which I shall try to enumerate.
The budget shows the sales tax to be the greatest revenue producer. It is estimated that it will produce $115,500,000, and that, plus stamp and manufacturers' taxes of $38,000,000, gives a total of $153,500,000 or 33-97 per cent. I ask the Minister of Labour in the absence of the finance minister: does the sales tax help the unemployment problem? When the sales tax and the manufacturers' tax in 1929 brought a revenue of $81,500,000, or only 18 per cent, just a little more than half of what it is bringing to-day, the present leader of this government, who I am sorry is not in his seat at the moment, rose in his place and said, as reported at page 2706 of Hansard of June 16, 1931, with respect to sales taxes-and I say. Mr. Speaker, that the sales tax does not help solve the unemployment problem:
What do they disclose? They disclose that the burden of taxation is being placed upon the backs of the people least able to bear additional taxation. . . . What there is in the way of loss of revenue from such exemption will have to be made up by taxes raised in another way. Where does my right hon. friend expect to get most of his taxation?
The present Prime Minister was addressing his remarks to the present leader of the opposition.
Where does my right hon. friend expect to get most of his taxation? He expects to get it out of the sales tax and from the excise tax of one per cent on everything that comes

into this country. What does that mean? The sales tax, as we all know, bears most heavily on the great mass of the people-
He repeated! that twice, yea like Peter he repeated it thrice; so if I do the same I shall be forgiven. He said:
The sales tax, as we all know, bears most heavily on the great mass of the people. . . . and that additional burden is placed on the great body of the people through the sales tax and the excise tax of one per cent on everything imported.
The sales tax in those days was 4 per cent, and it produced $85,000,000. To-day it is 8 per cent, and it produces $153,000,000. It is just double to-day what it was then. Therefore if these words of the present Prime Minister were true then, they are doubly true to-day. Further down on the same page he said:
Talk about the "death knell of protection"!
He was referring to 4 per cent sales tax
This is the death knell of everything in the shape of freedom of trade.
If that was true then, it is doubly so to-day. The point I want to make is that this tax does not help solve the unemployment problem.
In like manner, Mr. Speaker, there is another tax that does not help solve the unemployment problem, namely, the income tax, and on that I should like to say a few words. Demagogues like to speak of the income tax in derogatory terms. I have seen them standing on a chair on a street corner and heard them shout: "Soak the rich!-Make them pay!"

speechtext:
The Prime Minister says he can hear me outside. Mr. Speaker, I wish you would open these windows so that the whole of Canada would hear. I was just saying that the Minister of Labour has placed 46.000 boys on the farms of Canada. At the same time, as I pointed out, we in this country have a surplus of butter of record proportions; and since the United States, applying their so-called reciprocal methods of conducting affairs with Canada,
[Mr. Harris.!
and exhibiting their usual generosity, have seen fit to place a duty of three cents per pound against our animal fats, and from 34 to five cents per pound against the vegetable products of all the British colonies-because Britain owns most of the countries producing vegetable oils-we in Canada are suffering greatly from the inroads of vegetable oils into our Canadian market. In the next two years our butter producers will find themselves in a very difficult position if the Minister of Finance does not carry out the suggestion which is indicated in his budget speech, where he says:
The tariff board will have ready in the near future reports on other matters referred to it, and it is expected that these will be received in time for consideration by the government while the house is still in committee of ways and means.
I hope that this committee sits long enough to receive the reports on these questions from the tariff board. The evidence runs to 500 pages; there are forty items. The dairy farmers in the house number over one hundred, and if you multiply one hundred by forty speeches by five hundred pages perhaps we shall miss the coronation ceremonies but we may be able to receive the report, in the terms suggested in the budget speech, and be able to give considration to it in the committee of ways and means.
Now, as to the merits of the case itself, a tank steamer from Nigeria called the Swartzemmer, landed at Sorel in September of last year with 7,800,000 pounds of vegetable oil. It was entered on the records as vegetable oil "not for food," in like manner as 195,000,000 pounds is entered on the records of the bureau of statistics as not for food. But immediately we find it made into food. That is something which ought to be checked up. Only 8,000,000 pounds entered for food, and last year we produced
103.000.	000 pounds of edible shortening, sold to the housewives and bakers of Canada. The
195.000.	000 pounds entered "not for food" was refined and sold, at least 70 per cent of it, for edible purposes.
Getting back to this tank steamer at Sorel,
7,800,000	pounds was discharged in a few hours through a large pipe line into a tank on the docks. What does that mean? My Saskatchewan friends, how much butter do you produce? Twenty-three million pounds a year. In the seven winter months you produce 34 per cent of 23,000,000 pounds, and 34 per cent of 23,000,000 pounds is 7,800,000 pounds. The same weight of fat was on that steamer at Sorel as the 40,000 dairy farmers in Saskatchewan produce in seven

The Budget-Mr. Harris
months. Do you get the significance of that? If you do not, let me give you the full measure of this traffic. Imagine thirty tank steamers. If you cannot imagine that, you know what a tank car looks like; imagine forty-five trains of fifty ears each of 100,000 pounds capacity entering Canada-each and every year-one hundred and three million pounds of that production replacing the natural wholesome industry of this country, the butter fat industry, which makes work for your 46,000 boys who were put out on the farm replacement scheme.
It was requested that consideration be given to some amendment. The hearing before the tariff board closed on December 11, so that there has been plenty of time for a report. It should have been within the competence of the board to bring that report down. This parliament should sit here long enough to get that report and take some action on it, not only because of the situation between ourselves and Nigeria and other countries, but more particularly on account of the action taken by our reciprocating friends of the United States in placing an excise duty of three cents per pound against our product going into that country. If I had another hour I could tell the house how in the Nigerian climate they only have to shake down palm nuts from a tree, throw them into a pit and let them rot, press out the oil and then carry the oil to a tank steamer on the border of Nigeria. The tree does not need feeding as your cow in Saskatchewan does. They do not have to house the palm tree in Nigeria as you house your cattle in Saskatchewan. The native climbing the tree does not tear his trousers getting down, whereas our farmer friends in Saskatchewan must be clothed in the winter time. I could enlarge on all these differences between their civilization and ours, but that would perhaps be wasting time. They are empire colleagues of ours and they take this trade and our empire friends take this trade. But let me finish that other story. When he gets these nuts down out of the tree the meat on the outside gives 60 pounds of fat and the inside kernel yields 40 per cent, while the poor man who strips the cow only gets 3i per cent of fat out of his milk. This is a matter that should be given consideration.
Some will say: That is all bound up in the empire trade agreement; why was not something done about it before? In 1933 the traffic was only 91,000,000 pounds, but in four short years it has grown to 224,000,000. The act of the United States in this regard has brought the matter forcibly to the attention of the National Dairy Council of Canada and 31111-91
they are greatly alarmed about it. The opportunity to do something about it should be seized. The Britishers who received these cargoes of nuts on the west coast of England to the amount last year of 1,762,000 long tons do not mind what tax or duty you put against that product as long as you give them the preference. A preference of ten per cent a few short years ago diverted all that trade of pressing to the United Kingdom. The presser there is content,-it is on the records somewhere-provided he gets his margin of preference.
It may be argued: But you will raise the cost of living, the cost of these shortening and other products by the amount of duty you put on. That condition does not obtain in the United States to-day. I have under my hand five copies of invoices of which I took photographs in New York two weeks ago, of the Ward Baking Company, sold to their bakers, and I found the price to be 11 i cents, whereas Proctor and Gamble of Hamilton sold it the same week in Kitchener at 13 cents. In Columbus, Ohio, another firm sold a half-carload at 12 cents a pound, while at the same time, to another firm in Canada, a similar product, 100 per cent vegetable, was sold at 11J cents a pound. It was sold in Chicago at 111 cents and in Hamilton at 13 cents. And mark this carefully; let our baker and consumer friends get this idea clearly in their minds. Right on the body of this invoice, which shows the price to be 11| cents per pound, is a clause which says:
If the Bailey amendment is found to be unconstitutional and if this processing tax or excise tax or duty is collected back from the government, then we will reduce the price of this invoice accordingly and return to you the collection we made from the government less the incidental cost of collection.
What does that mean? That means that the manufacturer there gets 7-} cents for his product that he sells to the Ward Baking Company in Chicago and in Columbus, Ohio, while our baker here is paying the full 111 cents or 13 cents as the case may be. So that argument falls to the ground. True, to an extent it would add a little to the cost. But there is another observation that I should like to make. The revenue resulting to this country if the government saw fit to do just seventy-five per cent of what the United States did on June 20 of last year-it became law on August 20, 1936-would amount to $9,449,000, according to the rebuttal evidence put in at the tariff board hearing a few weeks ago.
But it may be said, the material would not come in then. It would still come in, but not to so large an amount. I remember in

this house twelve or fourteen years ago hearing the representations made with regard to oleomargarine. In those days we were worrying about a production of 5,500,000 pounds. To-day we are faced with a production of
103.000.	000 pounds, which will increase to
120.000.	000 pounds this year. In those days we were not worried about a surplus of butter and finding a market for it. To-day we have a surplus of 25,000.000 pounds.

subtopic: THE BUDGET-SUSPENSION OP STANDING ORDER 28 FOR SITTINGS OP MARCH 4 AND 5
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the house would allow me to put a motion that will ensure the debate continuing on Thursday and Friday if necessary. I move:
That standing order 28 respecting the committee of ways and means be suspended for the sittings of Thursday, 4th March, and Friday, 5th March, 1937.
If this motion were not adopted the Speaker would leave the chair on those days and the debate could not proceed.

Motion agreed to.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the house adjourned at 11.03 p.m.
